value_chain_position: royalty/streaming pure-play - no operating costs, direct claim on physical ounces produced by third-party mines
cost_curve_verified: Disagree on the number, agree on the conclusion: the deterministic proxy shows a trailing operating margin of 102.85% (top-decile band), which is arithmetically impossible and comes from non-cash gains including a $54 million mark-up on the Osisko Development stake in the third quarter of 2025; the company-reported cash margin - the right measure for a royalty company, which has no all-in sustaining cost - is 96.8% in the second quarter of 2026 (8 July 2026 release) and 96.7% for full-year 2025, still the best in its peer group, but cleaning the figure lifts the trailing enterprise-value-to-cash-earnings multiple from about 16 times to about 20 times.
gm_trajectory: Flat at the ceiling while revenue climbs: cash margin was 96.7% on $277.4 million of 2025 revenue and 96.8% on $102.8 million in the first quarter of 2026 and $97.8 million in the second, so margin cannot expand with revenue here - the only variable that moves earnings is the metal price, which is why a royalty book converts almost every dollar of price change straight into cash.
bull_thesis:
OR Royalties owns one of the cleanest business models in mining and is priced today as if it were an ordinary miner. It holds contractual claims - net smelter return royalties (a fixed percentage of a mine's revenue) and streams (the right to buy metal at a fixed low price) - on 23 to 24 paying mines run by other people. It pays none of the mining costs, funds none of the capital spending, and absorbs none of the cost inflation that has eaten operating miners' margins through this cycle. The proof is a cash margin of 96.8% in the second quarter of 2026, essentially unchanged from 96.7% in 2025 and from every quarter before it. Wheaton Precious Metals, the sector benchmark, does not match it.

The growth is already bought and paid for, which is rare. Management guided 80,000 to 90,000 gold-equivalent ounces for 2026 and 120,000 to 135,000 for 2030 - roughly 50% more ounces - and the assets that deliver it are already owned: the Namdini mine in Ghana (the royalty consolidated to a full 2% in January 2026 for up to $103.5 million), Buenaventura's San Gabriel mine in Peru (a 1.5% royalty inside the $115 million Gold Fields portfolio bought in February 2026), Ramelius's Dalgaranga in Western Australia (first ore delivered to the Mt Magnet plant in February 2026), and the expanded Spring Valley royalties in Nevada (the $168 million Terraco acquisition, closed in April 2026). Getting from here to 2030 does not require another cheque. As the chief executive put it in February 2026, the company has "the luxury of walking away from bad deals to wait for the right ones."

The asset quality is genuinely differentiated. Just under 75% of 2025 ounces came from Canada, the United States and Australia, and closer to 90% including Chile - the best jurisdictional mix in the peer group, and the reason this book should not carry the expropriation discount applied to royalties on West African or Andean-frontier ounces. The reserve lives behind the contracts are long: management describes underwriting "assets with 15- to 25-year mine lives," and the cornerstone, Agnico Eagle's Canadian Malartic, has an underground mine at Odyssey that Agnico still expects to carry the complex to a million ounces a year in the early 2030s.

The financial record corroborates the story rather than contradicting it. Net debt of just under $35 million at the end of 2024 was paid down to $10 million by the first quarter of 2025, to net cash by the second, and to zero debt by the third - each step delivered on the call it was promised. Operating cash flow set a record $245.6 million in 2025 and rose 56% year over year in the first quarter of 2026. Cash flow per share has risen eight years running. The dividend has been paid 46 consecutive quarters and was raised 20% in 2025 and 18.2% in May 2026, to $0.065 a quarter, which is roughly 20% to 25% of operating cash flow - covered several times over.

What has to hold for this to work. First, gold needs to hold somewhere near today's $4,154 an ounce rather than round-trip to its 12-month low of $3,353; a royalty converts price into cash almost one-for-one, so this is the dominant variable. Second, Agnico Eagle needs to restart the Barnat open pit on the schedule it published - remediation complete in the third quarter of 2026, mining resuming in the fourth. Third, Capstone's Mantos Blancos silver grades need to stop disappointing, which management has prudently guided flat to 2030 rather than assumed away. If those hold, a book generating roughly $336 million of cash earnings in 2027 on today's metal prices, growing to 120,000-plus ounces by 2030, deserves the 20-to-21-times multiple its senior peers carry, and the shares are worth materially more than $31.19.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require the business to be bad. It requires only that the price already reflects the business, that the cornerstone asset has a two-year hole in it, and that management spent the balance sheet at the top of the cycle. All three are true today.

Start with the cornerstone, because it is the largest royalty in the book by a wide margin. On 1 July 2026 a rock mass movement occurred along the north wall of the Barnat open pit at Canadian Malartic. Agnico Eagle suspended mining, and said the same week it expects to lose 60,000 to 80,000 ounces of gold in the second half of 2026 and up to approximately 150,000 ounces a year in both 2027 and 2028. At OR's 5% Barnat royalty that is roughly 3,000 to 4,000 ounces this year and up to 7,500 ounces a year in 2027 and 2028 - about 8% of a mid-range year, removed from precisely the two years that were supposed to bridge to the 2030 target. Worse for a royalty holder specifically: while the pit is shut the mill is being fed low-grade stockpile, and a net smelter return royalty is paid on the revenue the mine actually earns, so low-grade feed is a direct revenue cut, not a timing difference. OR's response, published the same day, was that its "2026 gold equivalent ounce delivery guidance range, as well as its 5-year outlook, remain unchanged." The 2026 claim survives only at the bottom of the 80,000-to-90,000 range: the first half delivered 43,497 ounces, and a flat second half less the Barnat drag lands around 81,000 to 82,000. The five-year claim does not survive the arithmetic in the middle years at all.

Second, the capital discipline that was the entire investment case in 2025 has been reversed. Management spent the February 2026 call celebrating restraint - "OR Royalties transacted on only just $25 million in royalty and stream acquisitions" while the sector did $9.3 billion - and then committed $438.5 million across four transactions in the following weeks, plus up to $96 million to Canadian Copper, a Canadian Securities Exchange-listed base-metals developer, in April. Those cheques were written with gold between roughly $4,500 and $5,600 an ounce. Gold is $4,154 today; silver has fallen from a 12-month high of $121 to $60. Buying a royalty is buying a claim on a metal price, and these were bought near the high. The balance-sheet consequence is already visible: $90.6 million of net cash at 31 March 2026 became $139.4 million of net debt at 30 June - a $230 million swing in one quarter, with the Terraco purchase funded by drawing the revolving credit facility. Any valuation that still adds back net cash, including the screener bundle's own instruction to do so, is a quarter and a sign out of date.

Third, the shares are not cheap once the earnings figure is cleaned. The trailing enterprise-value-to-earnings multiple of 15.7 times flatters, because trailing earnings include non-cash gains - most visibly a $54 million revaluation of the Osisko Development stake in the third quarter of 2025 - which is why the implied margin exceeds 100%. On a cash basis the multiple is about 20 times, the same as Franco-Nevada at 20.6 and Wheaton at 21.0, and above Royal Gold at 17.5 and Triple Flag at 15.1. OR has lower returns than Wheaton (13.9% return on invested capital against 18.1%), a smaller and more concentrated asset base, and thinner trading liquidity at roughly $10 million a day. There is no discount here to harvest.

Fourth, the downside is arithmetic, and the torque cuts both ways. A 10% move in the metal swings cash earnings about 9.7% - roughly $33 million on a $336 million base - in either direction. Gold falling from $4,154 to its 12-month low of $3,400 is an 18% move, worth about $59 million of lost cash earnings, and royalty multiples compress as the metal falls rather than holding. Take volumes to 85,000 ounces (the Barnat hole offsetting the ramp-ups), take the multiple to 15.5 times, and the equity is worth about $20 a share - roughly a third below today's price. There is no structural floor to catch it: no deal terms, no tender, and the net-cash cushion has been spent.

What would confirm the bear. Gold breaking below roughly $3,800 an ounce. A slip in the Barnat remediation timetable past the fourth quarter of 2026. A 2027 guidance range published in February 2027 that is flat or down against 2026 - which would concede the two-year hole management has so far declined to acknowledge. Or a fifth acquisition financed with equity rather than the revolver, which would tell you the balance sheet is no longer the strategic advantage it was described as.
sop_bull: Favorable case, about $45 a share on roughly 187.6 million shares. Assumes gold recovers to its 200-day average of about $4,590 an ounce, silver to a 65-to-1 ratio, Barnat restarts on schedule in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the 2027-2028 loss lands at the low end, and the owned growth delivers about 105,000 ounces by 2028. Parts: (1) the producing royalty and stream book - 105,000 ounces at $4,590 is $482 million of revenue, a 97% cash margin leaves $467 million, less about $36 million of corporate cash costs gives $431 million of cash earnings; at 21 times, the multiple Wheaton and Franco-Nevada carry today, that is $9.05 billion, discounted two years at 8% to $7.76 billion, or $41.37 a share; (2) development royalties outside the 2030 outlook - Cariboo, the expanded Spring Valley position, Cascabel minimum payments, Hermosa/Taylor, Windfall, Upper Beaver and Marimaca, which management sizes in aggregate at 20,000 to 30,000 additional ounces - weighted at about 60% and discounted, $600 million or $3.20 a share; (3) the investment portfolio recovering toward the $210.5 million carried at 31 March 2026, taken at $250 million or $1.33 a share; (4) less net debt paid down out of free cash flow to about $100 million, minus $0.53 a share. Sum: about $8.51 billion, or $45.37 a share.
sop_bear: Adverse case, about $20 a share, assuming the precious-metals chain turns against it. Gold round-trips to its 12-month low of about $3,400 an ounce, silver settles at an 85-to-1 ratio, the Barnat hole of up to 7,500 ounces a year persists through 2028 and offsets the San Gabriel, Dalgaranga and Namdini ramp-ups, and the sector's multiples compress with the metal. Parts: (1) the producing book - 85,000 ounces at $3,400 is $289 million of revenue, a 97% cash margin leaves $280 million, less $34 million of corporate cash costs gives $246 million of cash earnings; at 15.5 times, the low end of where Triple Flag trades in today's stronger tape, that is $3.81 billion, or $20.33 a share; (2) development royalties, worth little at $3,400 gold because none of them get financed there, $80 million or $0.43 a share; (3) the investment portfolio halving again from today - the Osisko Development stake is already at $2.28 a share against a 12-month high of $4.795 - taken at $80 million or $0.43 a share; (4) less net debt drifting to about $180 million as the raised dividend is maintained through a weak tape, minus $0.96 a share. Sum: about $3.79 billion, or $20.23 a share. Cross-check against the deterministic torque proxy: a 10% metal move swings cash earnings 9.7%, so the 18% fall from $4,154 to $3,400 costs about $59 million of the $336 million base case, and cutting volumes from 92,000 to 85,000 ounces accounts for the remaining $31 million. The two methods agree.
sop_breakdown: Base case, about $35.80 a share before discounting and $35.00 after, on roughly 187.6 million shares, using today's spot metals ($4,154 gold, silver at a 69-to-1 ratio) rather than a forecast deck. (1) The producing royalty and stream book at a 2027 run-rate: 92,000 gold-equivalent ounces - the guided 2026 range of 80,000 to 90,000 stepping up as San Gabriel, Dalgaranga and Namdini ramp, less the up-to-7,500-ounce Barnat hole - at $4,150 is $381.8 million of revenue; a 97% cash margin leaves $370.3 million; less about $34 million of corporate cash costs gives $336 million of cash earnings; at 19 times, between Triple Flag at 15.1 and the seniors at 20.6 to 21.0, that is $6.39 billion, or $34.05 a share. This is 95% of the value: for a royalty company the producing book is the company. (2) Development royalties not in the 2030 outlook, risk-weighted to about a third of management's own 20,000-to-30,000-ounce estimate and discounted, $320 million or $1.71 a share. (3) The investment portfolio - roughly 14.3% of Osisko Development, worth about $47.7 million at today's $2.28 share price, plus other holdings, marked down from the $210.5 million carried at 31 March 2026 - taken at $150 million or $0.80 a share. (4) Less net debt of $139.4 million at 30 June 2026, minus $0.74 a share. The multiple is the judgement call: 19 times puts OR near senior-royalty parity, which its peer-leading 96.8% cash margin and best-in-class jurisdiction mix earn, and which its asset concentration, mid-tier liquidity and the 2027-2028 hole at its cornerstone argue against. At today's $31.19 the market is paying about 17.8 times - already most of the way there.
risk_reward: Poor at today's price. From $31.19 the adverse case sits at $20.00 and the base case at $35.00 - roughly three dollars of downside for every one of upside to fair value, with no structural floor beneath the adverse case because the net-cash cushion was spent in the second quarter of 2026 and there are no deal terms or tender to catch the shares. The favorable case at $45.00 only opens up if gold recovers to its 200-day average, which is a bet on the metal rather than on the company. This is a good business at a fair price, not a good price.
catalyst_status_note: The events that move this name over the next year are all third-party operator milestones guided by quarter, with no contractual payment to OR Royalties on any fixed date. First, Agnico Eagle's Barnat remediation: after the 1 July 2026 rock mass movement, the operator guided remediation to complete in the third quarter of 2026 with mining resuming in the fourth (Agnico Eagle release, 2 July 2026; OR Royalties release the same day). Second, Harmony Gold's updated long-term mine plan for the CSA copper and silver operation, guided for the third quarter of 2026 (OR Royalties fourth-quarter 2025 call, 19 February 2026). Third, Capstone Copper's Mantos Blancos Phase 2 feasibility study, guided for 2026 after slipping from the fourth quarter of 2025 (second-quarter 2025 call, 6 August 2025). The transactions that were supposed to force a re-rating have already happened and did not: the Namdini consolidation (29 January 2026), the $115 million Gold Fields portfolio (18 February 2026) and the $168 million Terraco/Spring Valley purchase (announced 24 February 2026, closed April 2026 on a credit-facility drawdown) were all completed, and the Toronto shares have fallen from a 12-month high of C$65.31 on 27 February 2026 to a US$31.19 New York close today. Per this lane's rules the status is descriptive only and carries no weight in the verdict either way.
peer_comps_note: Measured against the chain map's true competitors, OR looks cheapest in the group on the screen and is not cheap once the earnings figure is cleaned. On trailing enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: OR 15.7 times, Triple Flag 15.1, Royal Gold 17.5, Franco-Nevada 20.6, Wheaton Precious Metals 21.0. But OR's implied earnings margin on that basis is 108% - above the arithmetic ceiling - against 89% for Triple Flag, 79% for Royal Gold, 98% for Franco-Nevada and 88% for Wheaton, because OR's trailing figure carries non-cash gains. Restating OR to a cash basis (about $286 million of trailing cash earnings) puts it near 20 times on the balance-sheet-date enterprise value and about 21 times on today's, which is parity with Wheaton and Franco-Nevada rather than a discount, and a premium to Royal Gold and Triple Flag. On returns OR sits mid-pack: return on invested capital 13.9%, against Wheaton 18.1%, Franco-Nevada 14.3%, Triple Flag 11.6% and Royal Gold 7.6%. Sandstorm was excluded because the price feed's last trade timestamp is stale, and Uranium Royalty because it is a different commodity chain. The honest read: OR earns a senior-royalty multiple on margin and jurisdiction quality, and it is already being paid one.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market runs in both directions, which is why this is a watchlist name rather than a conviction call either way.

Against the bulls. The street is still marking OR off a net-asset value built on two assumptions that broke in the last five weeks. The first is a gold deck above today's spot. Scotiabank's $42 target dates from 14 July 2026 with the stock at $28.89 and the consensus sits at $40.33 - roughly 29% above the current $31.19 - while gold at $4,154 is 26% below its 12-month high of $5,626 and below its own 200-day average of $4,587. A royalty converts price into cash almost one-for-one; a net-asset value struck at a higher long-term deck is not a valuation, it is a forecast. The second is a Canadian Malartic profile that no longer exists in the middle years. Agnico Eagle published on 2 July 2026 that it expects to lose up to approximately 150,000 ounces a year in both 2027 and 2028 following the Barnat wall movement. OR's response the same day - that its 2026 guidance and its five-year outlook "remain unchanged" - cannot be true across 2027 and 2028 at a 5% royalty, which is roughly 7,500 ounces a year or about 8% of a mid-range year. Only the low target in the file, Jefferies at $34 on 6 July 2026, appears to have priced any of this, and even that was set before the full production impact was quantified.

The third street assumption we would challenge is the framing of the 2026 acquisitions as accretion. Four transactions totalling $438.5 million, plus up to $96 million to a Canadian Securities Exchange-listed copper developer in April, were committed with gold between roughly $4,500 and $5,600. The immediate effect is visible in the company's own numbers: $90.6 million of net cash at 31 March 2026 became $139.4 million of net debt at 30 June, a $230 million swing, with Terraco funded by drawing the revolving credit facility. This is the sector's oldest error - deploying at the top - committed by a management team that had spent the previous four calls explaining why it would not.

Against the bears, in fairness. The shares are down about 35% from their 12-month high while the operating engine has not moved at all: second-quarter 2026 revenue of $97.8 million at a 96.8% cash margin is the second-best quarter in the company's history, and first-half deliveries of 43,497 ounces are on pace for guidance. If the market is pricing a return to $3,400 gold, our own adverse case is roughly the price. It is not: at $31.19 the enterprise is about $5.99 billion, which is 78% of the way from our $3.8 billion adverse case to our $6.7 billion base case. The market is pricing something closer to fair, not something distressed - which is exactly why there is no edge here yet.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next two to three quarters, and it is an earnings-and-sentiment problem rather than a solvency one.

The immediate item is full second-quarter results, due within days - the company has reported the second quarter in the first week of August in each of the last two years (6 August 2025, 5 August 2026 for peers on the same cycle). That print will carry three uncomfortable lines at once: the first net-debt balance in more than a year at $139.4 million against $75.6 million of cash, a first full-quarter mark on an investment portfolio whose largest identified holding, roughly 14.3% of Osisko Development, trades at $2.28 against a 12-month high of $4.795, and the first management commentary reconciling "outlook unchanged" with Agnico Eagle's up-to-150,000-ounces-a-year statement.

The second half of 2026 then carries the Barnat hole itself: 60,000 to 80,000 lost ounces at the mine, roughly 3,000 to 4,000 gold-equivalent ounces to OR, which pushes the full year toward the bottom of the 80,000-to-90,000 range rather than out of it. Compounding it, while in-pit mining is suspended the Canadian Malartic mill is being fed low-grade ore from stockpiles. A net smelter return royalty is paid on the revenue the mine earns, so low-grade feed reduces the royalty directly - a detail easy to miss when a company says its guidance is unchanged.

Third, the silver side is unresolved. Mantos Blancos grade reconciliation has disappointed on five of the six calls in the file, and management has now guided the asset flat all the way to 2030 rather than model a recovery. Silver has fallen from $121 to $60 in twelve months. With silver at 30% to 45% of revenue depending on the ratio used, that is the largest single swing factor after gold itself.

What is not a risk: there is no maturity wall. The revolving credit facility is $650 million with a $200 million uncommitted accordion, and roughly $215 million is drawn. The dividend, raised 18.2% to $0.065 a quarter in May 2026, costs about $49 million a year against operating cash flow that ran at a $245.6 million annual rate in 2025 - covered five times over. This company will not be forced to do anything. It will simply print softer numbers into a softer tape.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical forced-selling event here, which is part of why the shares can drift rather than flush.

The income-oriented shareholder base is the stickiest part of the register and it is not at risk. OR was re-included in the Canadian dividend-aristocrat index in late January 2026 on the strength of 45 consecutive quarterly dividends, and it raised the dividend 18.2% in May 2026 rather than cutting it. That base only liquidates on a cut, and a cut is nowhere in prospect at a payout of roughly 20% to 25% of operating cash flow.

The unstable money is generalist and momentum capital that arrived on the way up. The Toronto shares set a 12-month high of C$65.31 on 27 February 2026 and are now roughly half that; anyone who bought the February record-results-plus-three-acquisitions story is deeply underwater. Louisbourg Investments was already trimming in the fourth quarter of 2025, and the shares now sit below both their 50-day average of $32.26 and their 200-day of $36.65, with the 12-month low of $27.54 the obvious magnet. That is the cohort that sells into a disappointing second-quarter call, and it is why a flush toward the high $20s is plausible without anything fundamental breaking.

Elliott Management's 2.2 million shares, last publicly disclosed as of the August 2025 call, is roughly 1.2% of the company - a position, not a lever. Two board seats turned over in early 2026 (Kevin Thomson appointed and William Murray John resigned on 30 January; Patrick Godin appointed on 23 March), but nothing in the record links those changes to any shareholder campaign, and it would be wrong to price an activist outcome that no filing supports.

The one buyer that has shown up is the company itself, and it has shown up at the wrong times: C$50.8 million of repurchases across 2025 and a further C$17.7 million (US$12.9 million) in the first quarter of 2026, the quarter the shares peaked - against "a whopping 26,000 shares," in the chief executive's own words, when the stock was near $23 in 2024. If the buyback becomes genuinely countercyclical in the second half of 2026, that would be new information about how this board thinks.
forcing_function:
Three dated items, none of which pays OR anything contractually - which is the honest characterisation of the setup.

First and nearest: full second-quarter 2026 results and the accompanying call, due in the first week of August 2026 on the company's own two-year reporting pattern. This is the first forum in which management must reconcile its 2 July statement that the five-year outlook is unchanged with the operator's published two-year production loss, and the first look at the balance sheet since it flipped into $139.4 million of net debt. Either a credible reconciliation or an honest revision resets the debate.

Second: the Barnat restart. Agnico Eagle guided remediation to complete in the third quarter of 2026 with mining resuming in the fourth. A restart on schedule removes the overhang from the largest royalty in the book and is the single cleanest path back toward the base case. A slip past the fourth quarter extends the hole into 2029 and validates the adverse case.

Third: the two silver milestones that govern 30% to 45% of revenue - Harmony Gold's updated long-term CSA mine plan, guided for the third quarter of 2026, and Capstone Copper's Mantos Blancos Phase 2 feasibility study, guided for 2026 after slipping once already. Mantos in particular has been the recurring disappointment across the whole transcript file; a study that finally fixes the grade model would be genuinely new.

A fourth item worth diarising rather than trading: the 2027 guidance range and refreshed five-year outlook, due in February 2027. That is the date on which management either concedes the Barnat hole in the 2027 number or is proven right that it was absorbable.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a high-quality business at a fair price, and fair is not enough to commit capital today. The recommendation is to wait for the wash-out, with a specific level rather than a vague one.

What is genuinely good here is not in dispute. OR Royalties owns contractual claims on 23 to 24 mines it does not operate and does not fund, and it converts 96.8% of revenue to cash - the best margin in a peer group that includes Wheaton Precious Metals and Franco-Nevada. Just under 75% of its ounces come from Canada, the United States and Australia, the best jurisdictional mix in the sector. The growth to 2030 - from 80,000-to-90,000 ounces this year to 120,000-to-135,000 - is already owned rather than promised. The management record on the things it controls is strong: three consecutive calls in 2025 each delivered the next promised step from net debt to debt-free, guidance was met in 2024 and 2025, and 46 consecutive dividends have been paid with two double-digit raises in two years. This is a wide moat, and it is contractual rather than reputational: a net smelter return royalty is registered against the mining title, survives changes of operator (as it did when Eleonore passed to Dhilmar and CSA to Harmony Gold), and cannot be inflated away because OR pays no costs. There is no structural force eroding it.

What holds us back is three specific things, and the first two are new since June.

The cornerstone has a hole in it. On 1 July 2026 the Barnat open pit at Canadian Malartic - the source of the largest royalty in the book - was suspended after a wall movement. Agnico Eagle expects to lose 60,000 to 80,000 ounces in the second half of 2026 and up to approximately 150,000 ounces a year in both 2027 and 2028, which at a 5% royalty is up to 7,500 ounces a year, about 8% of a mid-range year, removed from exactly the years that bridge to 2030. OR said the same day that its guidance and five-year outlook were unchanged. The 2026 half of that survives at the bottom of the range; the middle years do not survive arithmetic. When a company answers a published operator disclosure with a reassurance rather than a number, that is the thing to test first, and the second-quarter call in the coming days is where it gets tested.

The capital discipline that was the 2025 investment case has reversed. Management spent the February 2026 call celebrating $25 million of restraint against a $9.3 billion sector, then committed $438.5 million across four deals in the following weeks and up to $96 million more to a Canadian Securities Exchange-listed copper developer in April - with gold between roughly $4,500 and $5,600 an ounce, against $4,154 today. Net cash of $90.6 million at 31 March became net debt of $139.4 million at 30 June. The screener bundle's instruction to add back $91 million of net cash is now a quarter and a sign out of date, and any valuation carrying it is overstated by about $1.20 a share. The buyback compounds the point: C$50.8 million in 2025 and C$17.7 million in the first quarter of 2026, the quarter the Toronto shares peaked at C$65.31, versus 26,000 shares when the stock was near $23 in 2024. This board buys high.

And the shares are not actually cheap. The screen's 15.7 times trailing earnings is an artefact: OR's reported earnings include non-cash gains, most visibly a $54 million Osisko Development revaluation in the third quarter of 2025, which is why the implied margin exceeds 100%. Cleaned to cash, the multiple is about 20 to 21 times - parity with Franco-Nevada at 20.6 and Wheaton at 21.0, and a premium to Royal Gold at 17.5 and Triple Flag at 15.1 - on lower returns than Wheaton and a more concentrated book. Reconciling the two sum-of-the-parts cases gives a base fair value near $35 a share, built almost entirely (95%) from the producing royalty book at a 2027 run-rate of 92,000 ounces on today's spot metals, at 19 times cash earnings, plus small credits for undeveloped royalties and the equity portfolio, less the new net debt. Against $31.19 that is roughly 12% of upside. The adverse case, with gold back at its 12-month low of $3,400 and multiples compressing, is about $20 - roughly a third lower - and nothing structural catches it, because there is no deal, no tender and no net cash any more.

So the timing call and the value call land in the same place for different reasons, and both land at neutral. On timing, the cornerstone is shut, the metal regime is neutral at best with gold below its 200-day average, the balance sheet just flipped, and results print within days - that argues for waiting. On pure valuation and forensic quality, ignoring all of that: clean books, a wide moat, a credible management record, and a 12% discount to fair value - a good business, an unremarkable price. Neither justifies a seat today.

The level we are waiting for is $27, near the 12-month low of $27.54, which would put the shares at roughly 15 times our base-case cash earnings and open a genuine margin of safety toward $35. The developments that would bring the entry forward without that price are a Barnat restart confirmed on schedule in the fourth quarter of 2026, or a second-quarter call in which management revises the 2027-2028 outlook honestly rather than repeating that nothing has changed. The development that would take this off the list entirely is a fifth acquisition financed with equity - which would say the balance sheet is no longer the advantage this company has spent two years telling us it is.
